newsitem.title: UK: Fowl pest in London as election turns chicken.
newsitem.headline: Fowl pest in London as election turns chicken.

text.p: Feathers were ruffled in Britain's election campaign when a chicken sent to embarrass Labour leader Tony Blair was upstaged by a headless bird who tried to roost in the ruling Conservatives' press conference.

"We think Mr Major is handling this election like a headless chicken," the nameless chicken, sent by the Labour-supporting Daily Mirror newspaper, said. "It was their idea in the first place to introduce the chicken thing into the proceedings but they don't seem to have a sense of humour when the tables are turned."

However, the yellow headless chicken nearly met a sticky end. As he tried to approach Prime Minister John Major, security men muscled him away and there was a minor scuffle. Asked whether he was seriously hurt, the chicken said: "Just a few ruffled feathers".

The outbreak of fowl wars was triggered by Major's accusation that Blair was "chicken" (afraid) of staging a television debate with him ahead of the May 1 election. The Conservatives said last night they would try to ambush Blair with a chicken at a press conference on Thursday launching the party's manifesto.
Labour, strongly tipped to win the election, replied by sending the Conservative chicken an accreditation form and saying the bird was welcome to ask questions at the press conference.
But, in a reference to Conservative MPs who have admitted taking money from businessmen to ask questions in parliament, Labour said the chicken would not be paid for any question he asked.

The Conservatives' chicken arrived in a chauffeur-driven car. He turned out to be a vegetarian who had never voted in his life. The two chickens squared up before the Labour conference but true to their reputation backed away from confrontation.

Inside the Conservative press conference, Major continued his line in day-old poultry gags, saying that Labour changed its policies so often that "one day they are fighting cocks, the next day they are chickens".
"We are trying to egg Mr Blair into a debate," he joked.
